The sentence supersedes the order as a whole and has no deferred effective date, so it took effect with the later order, signed 2011-12-19, and ends this clause on that date. Actor: Executive Order 13594. The alternative reading, that the clause's schedules governed pay until the later order's own schedules took effect under its section 7 (January 1, 2012, or the first day of the first applicable pay period beginning on or after that date), is disclosed in the rationale.

Section 8 states "Executive Order 13525 of December 23, 2009, is superseded." It supersedes the predecessor pay order by its own terms and has no deferred effective date, so it was performed when EO 13561 took effect on signing, 2010-12-22; nothing in the clause remained to be done after that. EO 13594 section 8 later superseded EO 13561 as a whole, which does not change this earlier end.

research_rationale:
EO 13561 of December 22, 2010 (Adjustments of Certain Rates of Pay; 75 FR 81817, Federal Register of December 29, 2010) sets pay rates for the statutory pay systems, the Senior Executive Service, executive, legislative and judicial salaries, uniformed services, locality-based comparability payments and administrative law judges by attached schedules, and in its section 8 supersedes its predecessor. Its section 7 makes Schedule 8 effective January 1, 2011 and the other schedules effective on the first day of the first applicable pay period beginning on or after January 1, 2011. Section 8 reads "Executive Order 13525 of December 23, 2009, is superseded." It is a self-executing supersession with no deferred effective date, performed when EO 13561 took effect on signing (2010-12-22); the project records the same kind of clause that way elsewhere. That clause's first end is 2010-12-22. Every other clause ends with the supersession of this order by EO 13594 of December 19, 2011 (76 FR 80191, Federal Register of December 23, 2011), whose section 8 reads "Executive Order 13561 of December 22, 2010, is superseded." That sentence is an express supersession of the whole order and carries no effective-date qualifier of its own; EO 13594 section 7, which gives its own schedules the effective dates January 1, 2012 (Schedule 8) and the first day of the first applicable pay period beginning on or after January 1, 2012 (the other schedules), speaks only of the "other schedules contained herein" and does not defer section 8. The supersession therefore took effect on signing, 2011-12-19, and that is the first end of the schedule clauses. Disclosed alternative reading: the schedules of EO 13561 continued to govern pay until the new schedules took effect (January 1, 2012 for Schedule 8; the first day of the first applicable pay period beginning on or after January 1, 2012 for the others, a date the held sources do not give). The lead-in of EO 13594 recites that Public Law 111-322 freezes certain pay schedules for civilian Federal employees at 2010 levels through 2012, which accounts for continuity of rates between the two orders without any continuing force in EO 13561. A by-number search of the held order texts for EO 13561 finds this order's own text and EO 13594 (Federal Register and American Presidency Project copies); EO 13594 is the earliest held instrument naming this order, and no earlier revocation, supersession or amendment is held. Searches: the dossier's three machine searches (U.S. Code release point 119-121, current through 2026-10-09; eCFR point-in-time search as of 2026-10-14 with GovInfo CFR bulk XML; Federal Register executive-order catalog disposition notes and operative sentences of 17,521 saved order texts) were chosen after reading their coverage notes, which carry no scope warning.
